Applications in Chronic and Ischemic Surgical Wounds The clinical application of HBOT in wound management has been most extensively explored in chronic and ischemic surgical wounds, where impaired perfusion and sustained hypoxia significantly hinder physiological tissue repair. Among these, diabetic foot ulcers represent one of the most studied indications for adjunctive HBOT. Multiple systematic reviews and meta-analyses have demonstrated that HBOT improves wound closure rates, accelerates epithelialization, and reduces the incidence of major amputations when incorporated into multidisciplinary treatment protocols [ , , ]. In addition to enhancing tissue oxygenation, HBOT has been shown to potentiate host immune responses and augment antibiotic efficacy, both of which are critical in infection-prone diabetic wounds. Chronic venous ulcers constitute another clinical domain in which HBOT has demonstrated therapeutic benefit. Persistent venous hypertension leads to microcirculatory dysfunction, leukocyte trapping, and progressive tissue hypoxia, ultimately resulting in refractory wounds resistant to conventional compression therapy. Adjunctive hyperbaric oxygen has been associated with improved granulation tissue formation, enhanced epithelial migration, and reduced ulcer surface area in patients with recalcitrant venous disease [ , , ]. These findings support the incorporation of HBOT as a complementary modality in advanced wound care settings. Burn injuries represent an additional area of clinical application. Thermal trauma induces microvascular thrombosis, edema formation, and compromised oxygen delivery within the zone of stasis. HBOT mitigates burn wound progression through vasoconstriction-mediated edema reduction, while simultaneously increasing oxygen availability to ischemic tissues. Clinical and experimental evidence suggests that HBOT may improve graft take, reduce infection rates, and shorten healing intervals in complex burn wounds [ - ]. Radiation-induced soft tissue injury remains one of the most established surgical indications for hyperbaric therapy. Chronic radiation wounds are characterized by fibrosis, obliterative endarteritis, and severe hypoxia, creating an inhospitable environment for surgical reconstruction. Evidence from controlled trials and systematic reviews indicates that HBOT enhances angiogenesis, improves tissue elasticity, and facilitates surgical wound closure in irradiated fields [ ]. The role of hyperbaric oxygen in this setting has become particularly relevant in reconstructive procedures, where vascular compromise limits healing potential. Beyond chronic ulcerative and radiation-related wounds, HBOT has been utilized in complex postoperative surgical complications, including wound dehiscence, necrotizing infections, and ischemic soft tissue defects. Clinical reports highlight improved infection control, enhanced tissue viability, and reduced progression of necrosis following adjunctive hyperbaric therapy [ , ]. These applications underscore the versatility of HBOT across diverse surgical wound etiologies. Collectively, the expanding body of clinical evidence supports HBOT as a valuable adjunct in the management of chronic and ischemic surgical wounds. Its ability to simultaneously enhance perfusion, modulate inflammation, and potentiate antimicrobial defenses positions HBOT as an integrative tool within modern, multidisciplinary wound care frameworks. The success of reconstructive procedures, such as skin grafts, local flaps, and free tissue transfers, depends heavily on adequate oxygen delivery during the early postoperative period. When vascular compromise occurs, tissue hypoxia rapidly precipitates necrosis, infection, and reconstructive loss. Adjunctive HBOT has therefore emerged as a valuable supportive modality, aimed at restoring tissue oxygenation and improving salvage outcomes. One of the principal mechanisms through which HBOT contributes to tissue salvage is the enhancement of microvascular perfusion within ischemic flaps and grafts. Hyperoxia promotes capillary angiogenesis, reduces interstitial edema through vasoconstriction, and improves oxygen diffusion across compromised vascular territories. These physiological effects are particularly relevant in the setting of ischemia-reperfusion injury, where oxidative stress and endothelial dysfunction threaten tissue viability following surgical revascularization [ , , ]. Clinical evidence supporting the use of HBOT in reconstructive salvage continues to expand. Reports across trauma and limb reconstruction literature have demonstrated improved graft integration, reduced necrosis progression, and enhanced wound stability when hyperbaric therapy is incorporated into multidisciplinary salvage protocols [ ]. Additionally, HBOT has shown benefit in crush injuries and complex soft tissue trauma, where microcirculatory collapse impairs physiological healing capacity [ , ]. The role of hyperbaric oxygen in complex wound reconstruction extends beyond extremity trauma. Necrotizing infections, ischemic postoperative wounds, and graft-compromised defects have all been described as clinical scenarios where adjunctive HBOT may reduce tissue loss and improve reconstructive readiness. Observational studies have reported enhanced infection control, improved granulation tissue formation, and higher rates of successful secondary closure following hyperbaric therapy [ , ]. Complementing these observations, broader narrative syntheses examining HBOT across surgical specialties have reinforced its role as a mechanistically active adjunct in tissue salvage. By integrating molecular, microvascular, and immunomodulatory pathways, HBOT contributes to graft survival, flap viability, and reconstructive success across diverse surgical domains [ ]. Such integrative perspectives underscore the expanding therapeutic scope of hyperbaric medicine within contemporary surgical practice. Breast and soft tissue reconstructive procedures represent additional areas where HBOT has demonstrated salvage potential. In the setting of ischemic mastectomy flaps or compromised nipple-sparing reconstructions, HBOT has been associated with improved tissue perfusion and reduced necrosis rates, supporting its adjunctive role in breast reconstruction salvage algorithms [ - ]. Collectively, the available evidence highlights HBOT as a valuable adjunct in surgical tissue salvage. Its capacity to enhance oxygen delivery, promote angiogenesis, modulate inflammation, and improve antimicrobial defense positions HBOT as a supportive modality capable of optimizing reconstructive outcomes in high-risk surgical scenarios. Clinical Outcomes HBOT has demonstrated measurable benefits across multiple clinical endpoints in surgical wound management and reconstructive care. Among the most consistently reported outcomes is the acceleration of wound healing. By enhancing tissue oxygenation and promoting angiogenesis, HBOT facilitates faster epithelialization, improved collagen matrix deposition, and more rapid progression through the proliferative phase of healing. Clinical studies evaluating chronic wound populations have reported shorter times to wound closure and higher rates of complete epithelialization when hyperbaric oxygen is incorporated into standard wound care protocols [ , , ]. Complication Reduction In addition to expediting tissue repair, HBOT has been associated with significant reductions in postoperative complication rates. Surgical site infections, particularly in ischemic or contaminated wounds, represent a major contributor to morbidity and reconstructive failure. Hyperoxia enhances leukocyte bactericidal activity and improves antibiotic penetration into poorly perfused tissues, thereby strengthening host defense mechanisms. Clinical observations across chronic wounds, burn injuries, and reconstructive procedures have demonstrated lower infection rates in patients receiving adjunctive hyperbaric therapy [ , , ]. Necrosis prevention and tissue preservation constitute another critical outcome domain. In compromised grafts and flaps, insufficient oxygen delivery often precipitates progressive ischemia and tissue loss. HBOT mitigates this process by improving microvascular perfusion, reducing edema, and supporting angiogenic recovery. Studies in reconstructive trauma, breast surgery, and complex postoperative wounds have reported reduced necrosis progression and higher rates of successful tissue salvage following HBOT administration [ , , ]. Amputation risk reduction represents one of the most clinically impactful benefits reported in the literature, particularly in diabetic and ischemic wound populations. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses have shown that adjunctive HBOT significantly lowers the likelihood of major limb amputation by promoting wound closure and controlling infection [ , ]. From a safety perspective, HBOT is generally well tolerated when administered within established pressure and duration parameters. Reported adverse events are uncommon and typically mild, including barotrauma-related otic discomfort or transient visual changes. Serious complications, such as oxygen toxicity and seizures, remain rare when standard therapeutic protocols are followed [ ]. Cost-effectiveness analyses, though limited, suggest that the upfront resource utilization associated with HBOT may be offset by reductions in reoperation rates, hospitalization duration, and long-term disability associated with wound complications and amputations. As such, HBOT may represent not only a clinically effective adjunct but also a resource-efficient strategy in high-risk surgical populations. Collectively, the available evidence underscores the multifaceted clinical impact of HBOT. Through its capacity to accelerate wound healing, reduce infection and necrosis, preserve tissue viability, and improve reconstructive outcomes, HBOT continues to solidify its role as a valuable adjunct within modern surgical care pathways. One of the most compelling aspects of HBOT is its versatility across surgical subspecialties. Although traditionally associated with chronic wound care and radiation injury, contemporary applications now extend into gynecologic oncology, reconstructive urology, and complex abdominal wound management. Clinical guidance frameworks have highlighted the utility of HBOT in managing irradiated pelvic tissues, postoperative dehiscence, and ischemic gynecologic surgical wounds, reinforcing its role beyond conventional wound paradigms [ ]. Similarly, case series within reconstructive urology have demonstrated improved healing and reduced complication rates in complex genitourinary wound defects following adjunctive hyperbaric therapy [ ]. Beyond reconstructive salvage, emerging literature has explored the role of HBOT within aesthetic and elective surgical settings. Systematic reviews evaluating HBOT in aesthetic medicine and anti-aging applications suggest potential benefits in tissue regeneration, postoperative recovery, and dermal remodeling [ ]. Complementary clinical investigations in facial aesthetic surgery have reported improved wound healing, reduced edema, and enhanced scar quality in patients receiving adjunctive hyperbaric therapy following rhytidectomy procedures [ ]. These findings support the concept that HBOT may extend beyond salvage therapy into perioperative optimization strategies within elective surgical practice. Scar modulation represents another evolving application. Prospective comparative studies have suggested that HBOT may influence collagen organization and fibroblast activity, potentially improving postoperative scar outcomes when compared with standard interventions, such as silicone sheeting [ ]. While preliminary, these findings raise important considerations regarding the broader regenerative implications of hyperbaric therapy within surgical wound remodeling phases. Predictive modeling and outcome stratification have also begun to emerge within hyperbaric research. Decision tree-based analytical approaches have been proposed to identify clinical variables associated with HBOT success, including wound chronicity, perfusion status, and comorbidity burden [ ]. Such predictive tools may facilitate more precise patient selection, optimizing resource allocation and therapeutic efficacy within hyperbaric programs. From a multidisciplinary perspective, the integration of HBOT with adjunctive technologies represents a promising frontier. Randomized and protocol-driven investigations combining hyperbaric oxygen with endovascular revascularization strategies for chronic limb-threatening ischemia aim to synergistically address both macrovascular and microvascular perfusion deficits [ ]. Similarly, combination approaches integrating HBOT with negative pressure wound therapy have demonstrated improved healing dynamics in chronic wound populations, suggesting additive regenerative benefits [ , ]. The systemic therapeutic reach of HBOT is further illustrated in inflammatory and gastrointestinal wound contexts. Evidence from observational studies and case series has documented successful application of HBOT in refractory Crohn’s disease-associated fistulizing wounds, where enhanced tissue oxygenation may support mucosal repair and infection control [ , ]. chunks.content: Introduction Cardiovascular surgeries can improve patients’ survival rate, restore their cardiovascular function and, most importantly, enhance their quality of life. Various cardiovascular surgeries, such as cardiac valve replacements, coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG), and heart transplants, are widely used in our daily lives. For example, valve replacement and myocardial revascularization are the most common surgeries performed on Brazilian adults. Moreover, various postoperative complications accompany these surgeries ( ). These include air embolism, sternal wound infection, postoperative cognitive dysfunction (POCD), hypoxic encephalopathy, atrial fibrillation, and pericardial effusion. These complications strongly affect patient survival rates and the length of hospital stay. Timely application of multifactorial nonpharmacologic and pharmacologic treatments can improve patient prognosis to some extent. Hyperbaric oxygen (HBO) involves taking in 100% oxygen at an elevated pressure above 1 absolute atmospheric pressure (ATA; 1 ATA = 101.325 kPa). It can increase internal oxygen partial pressure and increase the blood solubility of oxygen to elicit diverse therapeutic effects. HBO is widely used in clinical applications, including carbon monoxide poisoning, decompression sickness, radiation injury, and ischemic disease. This review focuses on the application of HBO in preconditioning and therapy for cardiovascular postoperative complications ( ). Search Strategy The authors used the terms “cardiovascular surgery” and “cardiac surgery” together with “complications” to search for literature in the PubMed database from January 1965 to December 2024. We are aware of common cardiovascular postoperative complications, such as postoperative cognitive dysfunction, hemorrhagic transformation, myocardial ischemia‒reperfusion injury, acute kidney injury, hypoxic encephalopathy, air embolism, wound infection, infective endocarditis, low cardiac output syndrome, sudden sensorineural hearing loss, and heart failure. These complications were used as new search terms. They were searched separately and screened on the basis of their relevance to obtain literature introducing the etiology and pathophysiology of these complications. After that, we retrieved these complication terms together with the term “hyperbaric oxygen” and further screened them by reading the literature titles and abstracts. Ultimately, we used these articles to elucidate the mechanism and efficacy of hyperbaric oxygen therapy for these complications. Application of Hyperbaric Oxygen Preconditioning in Cardiovascular Surgery HBO preconditioning refers to exposure to HBO before noxious stimulation to provide a prophylactic condition. Research has shown that it may imitate hypoxic preconditioning and induce ischemic tolerance to attenuate ischemia‒reperfusion injury without adverse effects. The application of HBO preconditioning in cardiovascular surgery is shown in . The mechanism of HBO preconditioning might involve the activation of antioxidant enzymes and related genes in the central nervous system, including catalase, superoxide dismutase, and nitric oxide synthase. Then, increased nitric oxide can initiate the nitric oxide/protein kinase G pathway by activating soluble guanylate cyclase, ultimately leading to the inhibition of the MPTP and a reduction in cell death. It can also stabilize glucose levels and decrease the lactate/pyruvate ratio and glycerol levels in the infarcted area while restricting the increase in glutamate levels. Increasing energy metabolism and reducing glutamate levels are crucial factors contributing to the neuroprotective effects of HBO preconditioning. An animal experiment indicated that daily 1 hour HBO preconditioning with 2 ATA for 5 days enhances the tolerance of cerebral ischemic neurological injury in hamsters; this phenomenon is closely associated with heat shock protein 72. In another clinical study involving newborns as subjects, daily HBO preconditioning with 2.5 ATA for 2.5 hours reduced the infarction area by inhibiting caspase-3 and caspase-9 activities. Effects of hyperbaric oxygen preconditioning on cognitive dysfunction POCD is a common complication following cardiovascular surgery. Research has shown that the incidence of POCD can reach 40% within 1 week and 17% within 3 months after cardiovascular surgery. It usually represents a decrease in memory, attention and cognitive performance. According to Gao et al.’s study, the mechanism of POCD might involve neuroinflammation caused by surgery, and central cholinergic deficiency is also an essential reason. HBO preconditioning is a useful method for POCD treatment. It has been shown to enhance postoperative cognitive function and reduce the occurrence of POCD. HBO preconditioning can also produce effective cardiovascular protection, ameliorate patients’ attention dysfunction and improve their spatial learning and memory skills. Alex et al. indicated that the plasma concentrations of neurological injury markers, such as soluble E-selectin, CD18, and heat shock protein 70, in patients who underwent HBO preconditioning before surgery were significantly lower than those in the control group. The decreases in these markers indicate that HBO preconditioning has cerebral and cardioprotective effects. Sun et al. indicated that HBO preconditioning can greatly ameliorate the serum concentration of proinflammatory cytokines, e.g., caspase-3, and improve the integrity of the blood‒brain barrier (BBB). Animal experiments have shown that Sirt1 may be an important molecular target for HBO preconditioning. Hyperbaric oxygen preconditioning on hemorrhagic transformation Hemorrhagic transformation (HT) is a common complication that occurs after AIS, while cardioembolic stroke is related to the highest frequency of HT. HT refers to the conversion of ischemic brain tissue into hemorrhagic lesions. It is usually accompanied by vascular leakage, resulting in brain injury. According to a previous study, HT has a morbidity of 42% in patients who have prosthetic valve endocarditis. Postoperative complications of cardiovascular surgery, such as atrial fibrillation and myocardial infarction, are critical factors related to HT. The possible reason is that these complications may exacerbate hypoperfusion. HBO preconditioning is a noteworthy method for HT treatment ( ). It can improve BBB permeability and neurological function and decrease the incidence of HT after AIS. The mechanism of HBO preconditioning might be related to the increase in hypoxia inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α). HIF-1α is a specific transcription factor that becomes active under hypoxic conditions. Under normal circumstances, it undergoes proline hydroxylation by proline hydroxylase and subsequent ubiquitination and degradation by the proteasome. Under hypoxic conditions, reduced proline hydroxylase activity prevents normal hydroxylation and degradation of HIF-1α, leading to its accumulation along with HIF-1β; these then bind together to induce the activation of hypoxia adaptation genes within the cell nucleus. The oxygen content decreased to a normal level at 21% after HBO preconditioning. This leads to relatively hypoxic conditions in brain tissues, which can promote the production of HIF-1α. The cycle of hyperoxia followed by hypoxia caused by repeated HBO preconditioning may contribute to the accumulation of HIF-1α. Hyperbaric oxygen preconditioning on myocardium ischemia–reperfusion injury Acute myocardial infarction (AMI) is a worldwide disease that threatens human health. The best treatment for acute myocardial infarction is timely reperfusion therapy, such as percutaneous coronary intervention and CABG. However, reperfusion therapy itself can induce myocardium ischemia‒reperfusion injury (MIRI), causing further death of myocardial cells and worsening patient prognosis. Effective interventions for MIRI prevention are urgently needed. Luckily, HBO preconditioning might be useful for MIRI treatment. A previous study revealed that HBO preconditioning (2 ATA, four times a day) 5 days before surgery can mitigate the degree of hemorrhage, necrosis and infiltration of neutrophils. It can also reduce the infarction area and reverse the elevation of left ventricular systolic pressure and left ventricular developed pressure caused by MIRI. In addition, HBO preconditioning can decrease the levels of inflammatory factors such as myeloperoxidase, tumor necrosis factor α, interleukin (IL)-1β and oxidative markers (malondialdehyde, protein carbonyl, 8-hydroxy-2-deoxyguanosine), which suggests that HBO preconditioning has anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects. Moreover, Yin et al. found that HBO preconditioning can activate the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/serine/protein kinase B (Akt) pathway and significantly increase the concentrations of nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2, heme oxygenase 1 (HO-1), and Akt. This activation helps protect patients from MIRI. In addition, it can ameliorate cardiac function and adverse outcomes. On the basis of a clinical study, HBO preconditioning does not confer a protective effect on patients undergoing off-pump CABG. However, for patients undergoing on-pump CABG, HBO preconditioning has the potential to mitigate the release of neurological and cardiac injury markers, such as S100 calcium binding protein β, troponin I, and neuron-specific enolase, and can activate a protective antioxidation pathway that depends on increased catalase activity. The data indicate that postoperative intensive care unit hospital stays are significantly shorter in patients who receive on-pump CABG with HBO preconditioning, accompanied by a decrease in composite cardiovascular adverse events. HBO preconditioning can induce oxidative stress, leading to an increase in reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation. However, part of its therapeutic effect could also be associated with increased quantities of nitric oxide synthase and heat shock protein 72 due to increased ROS concentrations. Research has shown that the serum concentration of troponin T, a marker of myocardial injury, does not increase after 1 hour or more of HBO preconditioning. Yogaratnam et al. These findings suggest that HBO preconditioning results in a smaller increase in troponin T following CABG and that troponin T levels tend to stabilize 2 hours after cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB), suggesting that HBO can mitigate myocardial necrosis and troponin T release. These results reveal that HBO preconditioning is a safe intervention method and does not lead to clinically detectable myocardial injury. Hyperbaric oxygen preconditioning in acute kidney injury Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common complication after cardiovascular surgery. It has a high incidence rate in elderly patients because of the aging of the kidney and nosocomial infection. Cardiovascular surgery is the second leading cause of AKI in the intensive care unit. Many factors in cardiovascular surgery can cause AKI, including ischemia‒reperfusion injury, oxidative stress, apoptosis, inflammatory reactions, and calcium overload. HBO preconditioning is regarded as an effective way to ameliorate AKI. It can improve renal hemodynamics by increasing renal blood flow and reducing renal vascular resistance. HBO preconditioning can also reduce oxidative and inflammatory reactions, decrease DNA damage and cell apoptosis, and even improve renal histological structure. In addition, phosphate clearance, creatinine, blood urea nitrogen and renal function were notably improved after HBO preconditioning. According to Nesovic Ostojic’s study, HBO preconditioning before the AKI model is constructed can increase the estimated glomerular filtration rate. The plasma antioxidant capacity measured by ferric reducing antioxidant power and 2,2′-azino-bis(3-ethylbenzothiazoline-6 sulfonic acid) assays was elevated at the same time. In the control group, 3-nitrotyrosine, an oxidative damage marker, was strongly expressed in the renal tubules and in the glomeruli, while its level in the HBO preconditioning group was significantly reduced. Nuclear factor-κB and histone H2AX at serine 139 were also abundantly expressed in the nuclei of proximal tubular epithelial cells in the control group, and their concentrations also decreased in the HBO preconditioning group. 3-Nitrotyrosine is a product of oxidative posttranslational modification and is associated with high levels of ROS. Histone H2AX at serine 139 is associated with DNA damage. These results suggest that HBO preconditioning ameliorates oxidative stress and protects DNA. HBO preconditioning can induce intermittent high oxygen-related hypoxia, leading to a moderate increase in ROS, which further activates downstream signaling pathways and upregulates antioxidant enzymes. Moreover, other studies have shown that HBO preconditioning can increase the expression of HO-1. The cell protective effect of HO-1 is related to an increase in the antiapoptotic proteins Bcl-2 and Bcl-xl and a decrease in the proapoptotic proteins caspase-3, caspase-9, and Bax. The overexpression of Bcl-2 can prevent the release of mitochondrial cytochrome c and reduce cell apoptosis. HBO preconditioning can also improve AKI histologically, such as making renal tubular epithelial cell lesions milder, decreasing renal tubular dilation, and decreasing Perodic acid Schiff’s reaction-positive casts. A previous study demonstrated that HBO can ameliorate AKI at the histological level and reduce damage caused by cell apoptosis. CPB establishes an extracorporeal circuit temporarily and substitutes the circulatory functions of the heart and lungs with the machine, allowing the heart to pause in the short term and creating a bloodless area and stationary heart for further precise surgical procedures. However, inflammation and coagulation reactions can be activated because of the contact between the blood and the operative wound as well as the CPB machine. These processes involve the activation of platelets, leukocytes and thrombin and can ultimately lead to systemic inflammatory response syndrome, edema, increased capillary permeability and organ failure. Moreover, inflammation and coagulation reactions can mutually promote each other, which makes the situation even worse. CPB also has other potential side effects, including MIRI, microemboli generation, endothelial injury and damage to the myocardial microcirculation. Therefore, CPB is a common factor contributing to various complications following cardiovascular surgery. HBO therapy can treat various complications after cardiovascular surgery, with specific pressures, times, and efficacies detailed in . Hyperbaric oxygen therapy for hypoxic encephalopathy after cardiovascular surgery Hypoxic encephalopathy is a common complication and the main cause of death and disability after cardiovascular surgery. The extracorporeal circulation process, decreased blood pressure, air embolism and cardiac arrest are important causes of secondary hypoxic encephalopathy. When brain cells lack perfusion, their basic oxygen demand cannot be met, leading to both metabolic and functional disorders in brain cells. Furthermore, this can cause cerebral edema and even trigger cerebral hernia. Depending on the degree of damage, hypoxia encephalopathy can manifest as different symptoms ranging from consciousness disorders to vegetative states. According to a clinical study, six patients with hypoxic encephalopathy after cardiovascular surgery received HBO therapy daily for 2 hours at 2 ATA. Three patients recovered consciousness after receiving 3, 6, or 11 sessions of HBO therapy and were ultimately essentially cured. The other three patients died due to severe clinical symptoms such as coma and limb movement disorders before receiving HBO therapy. HBO elevates the oxygen partial pressure and dissolved oxygen content in the blood. The arterial blood oxygen content can reach 5.3–6.4 mL/100 mL when pure oxygen is inhaled at 0.3 MPa. This value is 20 times greater than the arterial blood oxygen content at normal atmospheric pressure. HBO can also quickly improve the hypoxic state of brain cells and increase the oxygen diffusion distance. Timely HBO therapy can improve the oxygen supply capacity of collateral circulation, block and even reverse further functional deterioration of surviving brain cells located in the ischemic penumbra. HBO therapy can alleviate cerebral injury caused by hypoxia through other methods in addition to increasing the oxygen supply. For example, HBO can lower the serum concentration of fibrinogen and increase negative charges on the surface of platelets and red blood cell production to reduce blood viscosity and platelet aggregation ability. It can also reduce lipid peroxidation, accelerate thrombus absorption and restore the activity of calcium pumps to transport excess calcium ions from the cell, abating damage to brain cells caused by calcium overload. Research has shown that HBO therapy is able to decrease the expression of c-Fos in cells within the cerebral infarction area to prevent the extrinsic and intrinsic apoptosis of brain cells initiated by Bax. Through these effects, HBO plays an important role in hypoxia encephalopathy therapy. The mechanism of HBO therapy for hypoxic encephalopathy is detailed in . Hyperbaric oxygen therapy for air embolism after cardiovascular surgery An ultrasonic study revealed that almost all patients develop microscopic cerebral artery air emboli after cardiovascular surgery. Air emboli can be generated during extracorporeal circulation, and the main risk of their formation is the opening of the left ventricle and the aorta during surgery, such as valve replacement. Air emboli can reach the lungs via the pulmonary circulation and cause pulmonary embolism; they can also reach the limbs, brain and other parts of the body via the systemic circulation. Depending on the size and location of the air embolism in the brain, various clinical symptoms can manifest, ranging from confusion, coma, seizures, and cardiopulmonary failure to local symptoms such as unilateral or bilateral sensorimotor dysfunction. Ischemia and hypoxia may be direct damaging factors. Larger air bubbles can occupy the branching capillaries, causing the surface tension to increase and exceed the cerebral perfusion pressure, thus blocking or impeding blood flow. BBB dysfunction, water‒electrolyte imbalance and cerebral edema can lead to further damage. Air emboli can also induce endothelial injury, inflammatory reactions, and increased vascular resistance. Patients who receive HBO therapy inhale high-concentration oxygen to increase the oxygen partial pressure in the body and eliminate air emboli. At the same time, nitrogen in the air emboli can be replaced by oxygen in the blood, and then, oxygen is utilized by the surrounding tissues, thereby shrinking the air emboli. Blanc et al. indicated that patients treated with HBO within 6 hours after air embolism can achieve better outcomes than those treated with delayed therapy. These findings reveal the importance of early HBO therapy for air embolism. Blanc et al. also reported that HBO is more effective in treating venous air embolism than in treating arterial air embolism. Effects of hyperbaric oxygen therapy on cognitive dysfunction after cardiovascular surgery POCD is a complication that affects a single or multiple cognitive domains for a short or long period after surgery. The total incidence of POCD after cardiovascular surgery is as high as 70%. POCD can lead to reduced daily life skills, increased demand for nursing care and increased hospitalization costs, and the morbidity of dementia is also elevated. The development of POCD after cardiovascular surgery can be attributed to factors such as hypothermia and reduced perfusion during extracorporeal circulation, cerebral embolism, and inflammatory reactions. HBO preconditioning can alleviate POCD, and HBO therapy can also have a therapeutic effect even after POCD occurs. It can directly increase the partial pressure of oxygen, increase the dissolved oxygen content of the blood, and expand the diffusion radius of oxygen, thereby improving tissue and systemic hypoxia. The protective effect of HBO therapy on surrounding cells within lesion areas is related to its ability to expedite collateral circulation establishment, promote blood capillary regeneration and improve local microcirculation. Furthermore, HBO therapy can mitigate cerebral edema and intracranial hypertension by constricting cerebral blood vessels and enhancing vertebral artery flow. These effects increase the oxygen partial pressure of the brainstem ascending reticular activating system, thus promoting awakening among comatose patients. Effects of hyperbaric oxygen therapy on wound healing and infection after cardiovascular surgery Median sternotomy is a crucial procedure in cardiovascular surgery to approach the heart, but it can increase the morbidity of deep or superficial sternal wound infection and even rare yet severe inflammation and infection complications such as sternal mediastinitis and osteomyelitis. These complications can increase hospitalization expenses, prolong hospital stays and lead to death. HBO therapy can resist infection and promote wound healing and epithelialization. HBO therapy has good efficacy even when conventional debridement and antibiotic therapy are ineffective. Molecular oxygen can increase capillary angiogenesis and promote the generation of ATP, which is important in biosynthetic processes that occur in wounds. The hydroxylation of proline depends on the local oxygen concentration, and hydroxylated proline is the crucial raw material for the formation of stable collagen by fibroblasts. Ultimately, the continuously generated collagen can promote wound closure. These functions may explain why HBO therapy can accelerate wound healing. Prophylactic antibacterial effects could be achieved through HBO therapy after sternotomy. It can also reduce deep or superficial sternal infections following CABG. This effect may be attributed to the antibacterial properties of oxygen. Under HBO conditions, the oxygen binding capacity of hemoglobin is saturated; therefore, the blood oxygen-carrying capacity is improved by an increase in the plasma dissolved oxygen content. At high partial pressures of oxygen (100%, 3 ATA) over 24 hours, HBO has bactericidal effects on Pseudomonas aeruginosa , a common Proteus species, and Salmonella typhosa . Additionally, the lack of carbon dioxide enhances this effect. While the spores of Clostridium perfringens are resistant to HBO, HBO therapy can also prevent their germination. The bacterial killing mechanism of oxygen involves the reduction of molecular oxygen into superoxide anions, which have toxic effects. Elevated partial pressure of oxygen can enhance both enzymatic and nonenzymatic reduction reactions within bacteria. Superoxide anions also initiate the formation of other toxic ROS that contribute to bactericidal effects.” HBO therapy can also decrease the serum concentration of granulocyte colony-stimulating factor and IL-6 to induce immunomodulatory effects and reduce damage to patients due to inflammation triggered by infection. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy for infective endocarditis after cardiovascular surgery Infective endocarditis (IE) is a serious complication after cardiovascular surgery, and the mortality of patients without treatment is almost 100%. IE refers to infection of the inner surface of the heart, and cardiovascular surgery, such as valve replacement, is one of the common reasons for IE. According to the research of Kahrovic et al., among 576 patients who underwent aortic valve replacement, 1.4% developed IE. Other risk factors include intravascular catheterization, advanced age, and the use of cardiac implants. HBO therapy can treat IE as an adjuvant therapy through different mechanisms ( ). For example, HBO therapy can increase the oxygen content in biofilms to activate bacteria and shorten the bacterial division time. Therefore, antibiotic drugs, including tobramycin, β-lactam antibiotics and fluoroquinolones, can work better. Elevated oxygen levels can also enhance the respiratory burst of leukocytes to kill bacteria. HBO therapy increases the generation of ROS, which can oxidize and destroy bacteria, proteins, lipids, and DNA, thereby increasing resistance to infections. A study showed that HBO therapy can lower the level of vascular endothelial growth factor to limit the expansion of valve vegetation caused by platelet aggregation. The secretion of signaling molecules such as von Willebrand factor, IL-6, and IL-8 by endothelial cells is also repressed in HBO therapy, and the expression of anti-inflammatory molecules such as IL-10 is increased; as a result, the inflammatory response is suppressed. HBO therapy is also capable of preventing bacteria from producing toxins. Research has shown that Clostridium perfringens stops producing α-toxins when the oxygen partial pressure reaches 250 mmHg, and the oxidative stress caused by HBO therapy can lead to inactivation of the hemolytic toxins of Staphylococcus aureus . Oter et al. These findings suggest that the therapeutic effect of HBO is dose dependent, but the specific mechanism still needs further exploration. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy for low cardiac output syndrome after cardiovascular surgery LCOS is the most common and severe complication after cardiovascular surgery. Its incidence in adults ranges from 2% to 27%, and the incidence rate in children varies from 17% to 67%. The most common definition of LCOS is a cardiac index below 2.0 L/min/m and a systolic blood pressure below 90 mmHg and symptoms of insufficient tissue perfusion, such as oliguria, clammy skin and increased lactate concentration in the absence of hypovolemia. LCOS can lead to consequences such as atrial fibrillation, pulmonary complications, and acute kidney failure, and its mortality exceeds 20%. Yacoub et al. described HBO clinical treatment. A patient with preoperative pulmonary arterial hypertension presented typical symptoms of LCOS, including dyspnea and severe peripheral cyanosis 2 hours after surgery. The patient’s condition subsequently worsened, and typical symptoms of LCOS appeared, including cyanosis, decreased blood pressure, acidosis, and anuria. Blood transfusion and intermittent positive pressure ventilation therapy were ineffective for the patient, and it was ultimately decided to administer HBO therapy. The patient was sent to an HBO chamber and inhaled pure oxygen at two atmospheres. After receiving HBO therapy for 1 hour, the patient’s complexion began to improve, and after 12 hours, the patient regained consciousness for the first time and was able to start moving around. The patient’s condition improved significantly in the end, with only mild cyanosis. Acidosis was relieved, the arterial-blood pH increased to 7.37, and the patient began urinating after HBO therapy. The treatment process of this case revealed that HBO therapy has a significant therapeutic effect on postoperative LCOS patients with preoperative pulmonary arterial hypertension. HBO therapy helps maintain sufficient total available oxygen with low cardiac output by increasing the amount of oxygen dissolved in the plasma. It can increase the oxygen supply to the lungs and reduce pulmonary artery constriction and pulmonary arterial hypertension caused by hypoxia, thus reducing the right heart load. HBO therapy can also alleviate the systemic inflammatory response, reduce myocardial damage, improve cardiac function, and increase cardiac output. Although HBO therapy has been shown to have significant effects on the LCOS in certain clinical cases, few studies have explored the role of HBO therapy in the treatment of LCOS. Therefore, the exact efficacy of HBO treatment for LCOS still requires extensive clinical trials and further research. SSNHL refers to sudden hearing loss of at least 30 decibels at three or more consecutive frequencies within 72 hours. Patients may experience symptoms such as tinnitus, nausea and vomiting. Although SSNHL is not fatal, it may have a significant effect on the quality of life of patients. When frequency loss occurs within the range of 500–3000 Hz, which is the frequency range most commonly heard by humans, patients may develop reactions such as insomnia and anxiety. SSNHL after cardiovascular surgery is more common in males and is often unilateral, and the left ear is more susceptible to impact. The cochlea has a high oxygen demand and is supplied by only a single terminal artery, making it susceptible to hypoxia. Hypoxia leads to ciliary fusion of cochlear hair cells, edema of synapses and dendrites, sustained depolarization, separation of hair cells from the capsule, and microcirculatory obstruction, ultimately resulting in hearing loss. According to Bruschi’s clinical case report, a patient who underwent coronary artery reimplantation and replacement of the aortic root and ascending aorta developed nasal congestion and left hearing loss on the seventh day after surgery. The audiogram revealed severe sensorineural hearing loss in the left ear of 60 dB at 1000 Hz, and the patient’s condition was constantly deteriorating. While receiving conventional drug therapy, patients are also treated with HBO therapy, in which they inhaled 100% oxygen at 2.5 atmospheres once a day for 90 minutes. The patient began to recover after 10 days of HBO therapy, and his hearing returned to normal after 20 days. Patients might develop symptoms such as palpitations, fatigue, shortness of breath, and lower limb edema. A total of 10–20% of patients are readmitted after cardiovascular surgery due to heart failure. Leitman et al. found that HBO therapy can improve myocardial function in patients to treat heart failure. In their studies, patients received 90 minutes of HBO therapy at 2 ATA per day for 60 days. Transthoracic echocardiography was performed on all patients before and after HBO therapy. They reported that the left ventricular ejection fraction increased from 60.71 ± 6.02% to 62.29 ± 5.19%. The left ventricular end-systolic volume decreased from 38.08 ± 13.30 mL to 35.39 ± 13.32 mL. The myocardial function index decreased from 0.29 ± 0.07 to 0.26 ± 0.08. Simultaneously, improvements in function in apical rotation were observed. Conclusions On the basis of the preceding text, HBO clearly holds significant value in the perioperative period for cardiovascular surgery. HBO can be utilized as a safe and effective method for preconditioning patients prior to surgical intervention and as a therapeutic approach during postoperative recovery. HBO therapy has also been associated with a reduced incidence of perioperative complications, improved outcomes and shorter hospital stays. This not only benefits individual patients but also alleviates the burden on healthcare systems by optimizing resource utilization. However, some limitations should be noted. First, there remains a notable scarcity of literature specifically addressing its application within this field. Second, current studies may not be able to provide comprehensive data regarding dosage protocols, timing of administration and long-term effects posttreatment. Third, studies in these fields are not comprehensive and rarely involve the molecular mechanisms underlying the effectiveness of HBO therapy. In the future, further prospective clinical trials are needed to confirm the effectiveness of HBO in the perioperative period of cardiovascular surgery and broaden its clinical application. We believe that alongside ongoing advancements in technology, the potential benefits of HBO may extend far beyond current expectations.

chunks.content: Introduction Decompression sickness (DCS), colloquially referred to as "the bends," is a rare but potentially life-threatening condition that affects countless divers. With an estimated incidence of 0.4 to one case per 10,000 dives, it remains a clinically relevant outcome and concern for diving medicine. DCS occurs when the atmospheric pressure drops below the cumulative partial pressures of oxygen, carbon dioxide, nitrogen, helium, and water vapor in the vascular system [ ]. When this happens, gas bubbles can form in the circulation during decompression, leading to mechanical disruption of tissues. The resultant vascular obstruction and ischemia can cause edema and pain, which can mimic symptoms of cerebrovascular accidents [ ]. We present the case of a 50-year-old man who exhibited symptoms of underwater barotrauma and was later diagnosed with DCS. Case presentation A 50-year-old military veteran with over 20 years of combined recreational and military service experience and no prior history of DCS arrived at the Emergency Department (ED) with severe pain and noticeable swelling in his right shoulder. He had been engaged in a spearfishing dive, reaching a depth of 70 feet (approximately 21.3 meters). While underwater and handling his spearfishing gun, he experienced a sharp, intense pain in his right shoulder. Despite ascending appropriately, he noticed increasing swelling and worsening pain in the shoulder, which extended to the right anterior chest. The patient had severe limitations in his range of motion without any associated focal numbness or paresthesia. Before this dive and the subsequent retropulsion trauma from the kickback of his weapon, the patient reported a recent history of a mechanical ground-level fall to the right shoulder. Mild musculoskeletal tenderness was reported, but the patient denied any limitations to his strength, range of motion, or activities of daily living. Following a thorough assessment in the ED, the patient exhibited stable vital signs, and laboratory tests showed acute kidney injury (AKI) related to a previously treated case of nephrolithiasis. An X-ray of the shoulder revealed minor degenerative changes in the acromioclavicular joint. A CT scan simultaneously revealed the presence of gas within the proximal humeral diaphysis (Figure ) and extensive edema medial to the base of the coracoid process and nearby soft tissues (Figure ). Based on the patient's clinical presentation and imaging results, our initial diagnostic considerations included a potentially worrisome indication of DCS, necrotizing fasciitis in the context of underwater barotrauma, or other subcutaneous gas-forming organisms or conditions pertinent to the underwater nature of the injury. To refine our diagnostic approach, we considered our patient's presentation and recent diving history with a meticulous clinical and physical examination to scrutinize potential cutaneous/subcutaneous trauma in conjunction with his clinical presentation and imaging findings. Upon admission, the patient was started on maximum allotted oxygen supplementation via nasal cannula at a rate of 6 L; additionally, due to concerns regarding necrotizing fasciitis, empirical antibiotic therapy was initiated, consisting of vancomycin, piperacillin-tazobactam, and clindamycin (for its antitoxin effects against beta-hemolytic strep). In the absence of an operational hyperbaric oxygen delivery facility in close proximity, the decision was made to manage the patient medically using high-flow oxygen therapy, administering 15 L of 100% O 2 via a non-rebreather mask as an alternative treatment. While not standard for DCS, this approach has effectively treated mild cases in prior studies and reports [ ]. Further testing and imaging, including CT imaging, revealed that the patient had developed blood clots in the right axillary and brachial veins. Although this occurrence is uncommon in cases of DCS, it is scarcely documented in the literature. Some case reports have mentioned instances of portal and mesenteric vein thromboses being discovered after diving [ , ]. Based on these findings, the patient started anticoagulation therapy with therapeutic heparin. Upon reassessment of the patient's clinical presentation, which did not meet the qualifying criteria for systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) due to the absence of leukocytosis and fever, alongside a comprehensive imaging review in collaboration with our surgical colleagues, it was concluded that the patient was presented with an acute manifestation of DCS, as evidenced by cutaneous and musculoskeletal symptoms. Consequently, empiric antibiotic coverage was discontinued. Discussion DCS arises from the departure of depressurized gas, typically nitrogen, from tissues, forming obstructive bubbles and impeding circulation. This condition is commonly triggered by rapid tissue decompression during swift ascent from deep-sea diving, unpressurized aircraft flight, and extravehicular activities in space [ ]. Experts have classified the manifestations of this disorder into three types: type I DCS presents with skin, musculoskeletal, or lymphatic involvement; type II DCS manifests with symptoms of brain or spinal injury; and type III DCS presents with potentially fatal pulmonary complications [ ]. Various factors, including dehydration, patent foramen ovale, prior injury, cold ambient temperature, high body fat composition, and recent alcohol consumption, can influence the risk of DCS in individuals. DCS can be subdivided into different variants based on their clinical presentation and systemic effects. Type I DCS presents symptoms related to the skin, lymphatic system, or musculoskeletal system and represents the most prevalent form of this condition. On the other hand, type II DCS affects the nervous system and is linked to the presence of venous bubbles with right-to-left shunting [ , ]. Approximately 75% of individuals with DCS exhibit symptoms within one hour following the triggering event. Healthcare providers must conduct a prompt, targeted assessment and initiate immediate measures for stabilization. Even in cases where oxygen saturation levels are normal, it is advisable to administer high-flow oxygen to suspected DCS patients, as it can aid in the elimination of nitrogen gas pockets in the tissues [ ]. The clinical history of DCS typically includes rapid decompression, followed by manifestations in the skin, muscles, bones, joints, inner ear, brain, spine, and, rarely, the lungs. These symptoms may arise within minutes to several hours. Type I DCS commonly affects the shoulder joint, although any joint can be involved. Cutis marmorata, which can be localized or widespread, may also be present. Additionally, patients may exhibit lymph node swelling and pain. Type II DCS may present with the symptoms mentioned above, as well as headache, visual and hearing impairment, nausea, tinnitus, poor coordination, and, in some cases, altered sensorium [ , ]. Our patient's presentation, consisting of severe musculoskeletal and joint pain with swelling and without neurological compromise, aligns with the symptoms of type I DCS. However, the rare adjunctive presentation of coagulopathy in the axillary and brachial veins is an uncommon finding not typically seen in type I DCS [ - ]. Although our patient properly ascended from his dive, his prior injury to the right arm likely was a predisposing factor for his development of DCS. One could hypothesize that a disruption in the soft tissues from the fall on the right shoulder served as a nidus for gas bubbles to escape. Indeed, DCS in recreational scuba divers is low, approximately 0.4 to one case per 10,000 dives, primarily due to increased awareness and education about prevention in recent years [ ]. The most common presenting symptom of DCS is musculoskeletal pain, much like our patient experienced, followed by patchy paresthesia, motor weakness, and constitutional symptoms such as headache and fatigue. Ischemia and inflammation typically cause widespread tissue damage [ ]. Cutis marmorata, characterized by pruritic, netlike, red lesions, can develop in the skin. Patients may also experience pain in areas affected by bone and joint necrosis. Additionally, swollen and painful lymph nodes may be observed [ , ]. Symptoms are often vague and non-discrete. However, practitioners should maintain a healthy level of suspicion in patients who present with the above symptoms following a recent dive. Compliance with recommended dive tables, or ascension rates dependent on maximum dive depth, is the most effective way to reduce the risk of DCS, but this does not eliminate the risk [ , ]. This could explain why our patient suffered from DCS despite ascending correctly, according to the recommended guidelines. Other risk factors for DCS include dives deeper than 21 meters, dives conducted in cold water, dives in which divers physically exert themselves more than typical, and a history of DCS [ , ]. For our patient, age, recent illness, including recent hospitalization for nephrolithiasis, and immersion in cold fall-winter waters at depths above 21 meters were proponents for his development of DCS. For our patient, age, recent illness, including recent hospitalization for nephrolithiasis, and immersion in cold fall-winter waters at depths above 21 meters were proponents for his development of DCS. The diagnosis of DCS remains clinical mainly, as there are no specific lab values that definitively point towards the diagnosis. Imaging may suggest the diagnosis, but often, these measures do not meaningfully contribute to decisions about treatment and may even delay the diagnosis further [ , ]. Type I DCS may even be confused with systemic viral illness, systemic lupus erythematosus, presentations indicative of acute bacterial diseases such as gonorrhea and syphilis, new presentations of leukemia or lymphoma, and dehydration [ , ]. Type II DCS may be confused on initial clinical presentation to disease processes involving thermal stress, nitrogen narcosis, meningococcemia, multiple sclerosis, hypoglycemia, acute stroke, or inner ear barotrauma [ , ]. Treatment for DCS is often based on the severity of the patient's presentation, but standard measures include oxygen supplementation with the highest possible fraction of inspired oxygen available [ , ]. A definitive treatment for DCS is recompression in a hyperbaric chamber to reduce bubble volume by enhancing the diffusion gradient for inert gas from bubbles to dissolution in blood [ , , ]. A consensus has emerged that patients with "mild" DCS, primarily defined as musculoskeletal, cutaneous, or constitutional symptoms, can be effectively treated with oxygen supplementations without simultaneous recompression [ , ]. Our patient's clinical course adds evidence to this claim, as the patient presented with symptoms consistent with mild DCS and was effectively treated with 100% oxygen supplementation. However, it is strongly recommended that patients with any signs of focal neurologic deficits undergo recompression therapy as urgently as possible, and this is often complicated by the fact that divers do not present with symptoms until one to two days following their dive [ , , ]. Additionally, there are contraindications to hyperbaric oxygen therapy, namely, ear injury, pneumothorax, and any condition in which lung collapse may be possible [ ]. These conditions may concurrently manifest in divers as DCS, which presents a clinical fork in the road. Traditional, definitive management for DCS involves immediate administration of 100% oxygen, with subsequent transfer to a hyperbaric oxygen chamber facility if patients show signs of neurologic or respiratory symptoms [ - ]. Our patient exhibited solely musculoskeletal symptoms, so he was properly and adequately managed with 15 L/minute of high-flow oxygen supplementation. Significantly, our patient did not suffer lasting sequelae of DCS or develop new or worsening symptoms. Conclusions Our case highlights the necessity of maintaining a heightened level of clinical suspicion for DCS in individuals who have recently participated in dives or air travel. Compression sickness ensued despite the patient's extensive diving experience, adherence to proper ascending procedures, and preventive measures taken to prevent the condition. This was likely attributed to a predisposing shoulder trauma sustained days before the dive. Although the differential diagnosis was diligently broadened to incorporate the possibility of necrotizing fasciitis, the most probable clinical scenario pointed toward DCS. Owing to a high level of suspicion for this diagnosis, the patient received suitable treatment through high-flow oxygen supplementation, thereby avoiding enduring or long-term sequelae associated with gas embolism. The treatment protocol for DCS is contingent upon the severity of the patient's condition. The established standard involves the administration of oxygen, aiming for the highest possible fraction of inspired oxygen. Recompression in a hyperbaric oxygen chamber is the definitive therapy for DCS, facilitating the elimination of nitrogenous gas bubbles from the circulatory system and assisting in the dissolution of blood. The current consensus generally agrees that patients with "mild" DCS, characterized by musculoskeletal, cutaneous, or constitutional symptoms, can be effectively managed with oxygen supplementation alone, provided there is no clinical progression or development of new symptoms. However, if such progression or development occurs despite adequate oxygen supplementation, transfer to a facility capable of recompression therapies is warranted. This case underscores three crucial considerations for clinicians managing DCS: (1) It is necessary to consider DCS even when adhering to proper diving protocols; (2) the potential efficacy of high-flow oxygen therapy in the absence of hyperbaric chambers; and (3) the imperative need for a high index of suspicion for DCS in divers presenting with musculoskeletal symptoms in the absence of neurological and infectious causes.
